title: Rotten egg smell
h1: Why does my car smell like rotten eggs?
metaDesc: Car smells like rotten eggs or sulfur? Answer a few questions to see if it's the catalytic converter, battery, fuel or gear oil, and how urgent it is.
synonyms: car smells like sulfur when accelerating
car battery smells like rotten eggs
rotten egg smell when I hit the gas
intro: A rotten egg or sulfur smell usually comes from the exhaust system, most often the catalytic converter dealing with too much fuel. Less often it's an overcharged battery or leaking gear oil, which need different handling. Answer the questions below to find the likely source and how soon to act.
safety: If the check engine light is flashing and the engine shakes or loses power, pull over and turn it off. The catalytic converter can overheat and start a fire.
If the battery is hissing, steaming, swollen or leaking, don't touch it. Keep sparks and flames away.
If anyone has a headache, dizziness, nausea, confusion or unusual sleepiness with exhaust fumes, pull over safely. Get everyone into fresh air and call 911 from there.
If you suspect a fire, pull over safely and switch off the vehicle. Get everyone at least 100 feet away, clear of traffic, and call 911 from there. Leave the hood closed and stay away.

q_danger.q: Does either of these apply right now?

opts.a: The check engine light is flashing, or the engine is shaking or losing power
The smell is strongest at the battery, or the battery is hot, hissing, swollen or leaking

q_when.q: When and where do you notice the smell most?

opts.a: From the exhaust, mostly when accelerating hard, climbing hills or right after a drive
Mostly after filling up at one particular gas station, and it fades
Near a wheel or the middle or back of the car, with oily drips underneath
Along with the battery light, or lights that are unusually bright or flickering

q_cel.q: Is the check engine light on, or has the car changed how it drives?
q_cel.help: A steady (not flashing) check engine light means the car has stored a trouble code. Any auto parts store or shop can read it.

opts.a: The check engine light is on steady
It feels down on power, or rattles from under the car
No light, and it drives normally

result.title: The engine may be misfiring and overheating the catalytic converter
result.now: Pull over as soon as it's safe and turn off the engine. Have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If you see smoke or a glow under the car, get everyone away from the vehicle and call 911.
If the light stops flashing after a restart, don't trust it. Have the misfire diagnosed before driving any distance.
result.why: A flashing check engine light usually means the engine is misfiring badly. Unburned fuel goes into the catalytic converter and burns there, making it extremely hot. That causes the sulfur smell and can melt the converter or set fire to things underneath the car.

causes.name: Failed ignition coil or spark plug
causes.clues: Shaking at idle or under load, and the problem started suddenly.

causes.name: Leaking or stuck fuel injector
causes.clues: A strong fuel smell along with the sulfur smell, or black smoke.

causes.name: Overheated or damaged catalytic converter
causes.clues: Heat felt through the floor, or loss of power that gets worse as you drive.

shop: Code scan and misfire counter check
Ignition coil and spark plug test
Exhaust back-pressure test on the catalytic converter

result.title: The battery may be overcharging or failing inside
result.now: If driving, pull over safely and switch off the vehicle. Get away from the battery. Leave the hood closed and do not touch, jump-start or charge the battery. Arrange roadside assistance. If there is smoke or a suspected fire, move everyone at least 100 feet away and call 911.
if: If the battery is swollen, cracked or leaking liquid, keep everyone well away. Battery acid burns skin and the gas it gives off can ignite.
If the smell fades and the battery looks normal once cool, still don't drive it until the charging system has been tested.
If you see smoke or flames, get everyone well away from the car and call 911.
result.why: When a battery gets too much charging voltage or shorts inside, the acid boils and gives off a sulfur smell along with flammable gas. The battery can swell, leak or, rarely, burst. Common causes are a faulty alternator voltage regulator or a battery at the end of its life. A shop will usually test the charging voltage and the battery before replacing either.

causes.name: Alternator overcharging (faulty voltage regulator)
causes.clues: Lights that seem unusually bright, bulbs burning out, or the battery light flickering.

causes.name: Internal short in an old battery
causes.clues: The battery is more than 4–5 years old, or one side feels much hotter.

causes.name: Wrong charger or charger left on
causes.clues: The battery was recently charged with a home charger.

result.title: The charging system may be cooking the battery
result.now: With a sulfur smell and unusual lights or a battery warning, park safely, switch the vehicle off and keep away from the battery. Arrange roadside help or a mobile inspection before use. If you suspect a fire, leave the hood closed, get clear and call 911.
if: If you suspect a fire, pull over safely and switch off the vehicle. Get everyone at least 100 feet away, clear of traffic, and call 911 from there. Leave the hood closed and stay away.
Tell the technician which warning light you saw and whether the lights changed.
result.why: A sulfur smell alongside a battery warning or odd lighting can mean the alternator isn't regulating voltage correctly. Too much voltage overcharges the battery and makes it give off sulfur gas. Too little and the car can stall.

causes.name: Faulty voltage regulator in the alternator
causes.clues: Unusually bright lights, bulbs failing often, or the battery light on.

causes.name: Failing battery
causes.clues: The battery is old, starts have been slow, or there's crusty buildup on the terminals.

causes.name: Bad charging system wiring or ground
causes.clues: The lights flicker over bumps or the gauges jump around.

shop: Charging voltage test with the engine running
Voltage-drop test on charging wires and grounds

result.title: The engine may be running rich or the catalytic converter may be failing
result.now: Get the check engine code read and have the car checked within a few days. Avoid hard acceleration and long trips until then.
if: If the check engine light starts flashing or the engine shakes, pull over and turn it off.
If the car keeps losing power or the floor feels hot, stop driving it. A blocked converter can overheat.
If you smell burning or see smoke from under the car, pull over, turn the engine off and step away.
If anyone has a headache, dizziness, nausea, confusion or unusual sleepiness with exhaust fumes, pull over safely. Get everyone into fresh air and call 911 from there.
result.why: The catalytic converter normally turns sulfur in the exhaust into odorless gases. When the engine sends it too much fuel, or the converter is worn out, it can't keep up, and you smell sulfur. An engine problem left alone can also damage the converter, so a shop will usually check the fuel mixture and sensors before replacing the converter.

causes.name: Engine running rich (too much fuel)
causes.clues: Worse gas mileage, a fuel smell, or a code for an oxygen sensor or fuel trim.

causes.name: Worn or damaged catalytic converter
causes.clues: A catalyst efficiency code, a rattle from under the car, or power loss at speed.

causes.name: Faulty oxygen sensor
causes.clues: An oxygen sensor code with no other symptoms.

you: Have the trouble code read for free at many auto parts stores.
Note whether gas mileage has dropped recently.
shop: Code scan with fuel trim and oxygen sensor data

result.title: An occasional sulfur smell after hard driving can be the catalytic converter working hard
result.now: Try a different gas station for your next couple of fill-ups, and book a check when convenient if the smell continues.
if: If the smell becomes constant or the check engine light comes on, get it checked within a few days.
If the check engine light flashes or the engine shakes, pull over and turn it off.
If anyone has a headache, dizziness, nausea, confusion or unusual sleepiness with exhaust fumes, pull over safely. Get everyone into fresh air and call 911 from there.
result.why: Fuel naturally contains a little sulfur. Under hard acceleration the catalytic converter can briefly release some as a rotten egg smell, especially on newer cars or with certain fuel. If it's rare and the car runs normally, it's less likely to mean damage, but a code scan is the way to rule out a fuel mixture problem.

causes.name: Normal converter odor under heavy load
causes.clues: Only after hard acceleration, towing or long climbs, and it fades quickly.

causes.name: Fuel with higher sulfur content
causes.clues: It started after filling up at a new station.

causes.name: Engine running slightly rich
causes.clues: Gas mileage has crept down over time.
causes.against: If mileage and performance are unchanged, this is less likely.

you: Switch gas stations or fuel brands for a few tanks.
Keep track of your gas mileage.
shop: Code scan and fuel trim check

result.title: The fuel may be the cause
result.now: Fill up at a different station for the next few tanks and see if the smell goes away.
if: If the smell continues with different fuel, have the car checked when convenient.
If the check engine light comes on or the engine runs rough, get it checked within a few days.
If the check engine light flashes, or you smell it strongly inside the car, pull over and turn the engine off. That's no longer a fuel issue.
result.why: All gasoline has a small amount of sulfur, and some batches have more than others. The catalytic converter can't always clean all of it up, so a tank of higher-sulfur fuel can leave a temporary rotten egg smell.

causes.name: Higher-sulfur fuel batch
causes.clues: The smell started right after a fill-up and fades as you use the tank.

causes.name: Catalytic converter or fuel mixture problem
causes.clues: The smell continues no matter where you fill up.

you: Try a different station for two or three fill-ups.
Note whether the smell comes back with each fill-up at the original station.
shop: Code scan and fuel trim check

result.title: Gear oil may be leaking from the transmission or a differential
result.now: Look under the car for thick, dark drips, and book a check when convenient so the leak can be found and the fluid level topped up.
if: If the drips are steady or you hear new whining, grinding or howling from that area, get it checked within a few days. Running low on gear oil can ruin gears and bearings.
If the leak is near a wheel and there's oil on the brake parts, have it checked before driving. Oil on brakes reduces stopping power.
If you see smoke from under the car or smell burning oil, pull over and turn the engine off. Oil dripping on a hot exhaust can catch fire.
result.why: Gear oil used in manual transmissions, differentials and transfer cases contains sulfur additives with a strong rotten egg smell. A leak that drips onto hot exhaust parts or collects underneath can make the whole car smell.

causes.name: Leaking differential seal or cover
causes.clues: Oily drips near the rear axle on rear-wheel-drive, all-wheel-drive or 4WD vehicles.

causes.name: Leaking manual transmission or transfer case
causes.clues: Drips under the middle of the car.

causes.name: Leaking axle seal
causes.clues: Oil on the inside of a wheel or tire.

you: Put cardboard under the car overnight and note where thick, dark drops land.
Check the inside of each wheel for oily residue.
shop: Differential and transmission fluid level check
Brake inspection if oil is near a wheel

result.title: Often the exhaust or catalytic converter. Have it checked
result.now: Note when the smell happens and whether any warning lights are on, then book a check when convenient.
if: If a warning light comes on, the engine runs rough, or the smell is strong inside the car, get it checked within a few days.
If the check engine light flashes, or you see smoke or a glow under the car, pull over and turn the engine off.
If anyone has a headache, dizziness, nausea, confusion or unusual sleepiness with exhaust fumes, pull over safely. Get everyone into fresh air and call 911 from there.
If the battery is hot, hissing or swollen, turn the engine off and keep away from it.
result.why: The catalytic converter is a common source of a rotten egg smell, but an overcharged battery or leaking gear oil can smell the same. A shop can usually tell them apart with a code scan, a charging test and a look underneath.

causes.name: Catalytic converter or fuel mixture problem
causes.clues: The smell comes from the exhaust, especially after accelerating.

causes.name: Overcharging or failing battery
causes.clues: The smell is strongest under the hood near the battery.

causes.name: Gear oil leak
causes.clues: Oily drips under the middle or rear of the car.

you: Note any warning lights and what you noticed before parking. Avoid breathing fumes or approaching the battery or tailpipe.
